en.title: Modal verbs and il faut
en.goal: Conjugate vouloir, pouvoir, devoir and savoir, and understand when to use il faut instead of devoir.

blocks.title: Vouloir and pouvoir
blocks.body: Vouloir (to want) and pouvoir (can / to be able to) are two of the most used verbs in French, and they appear in almost every everyday conversation. You've already seen both in earlier units, without stopping to think about the full conjugation.
examples: Can I try on this dress?

blocks.title: Devoir and savoir
blocks.body: Devoir (must / to have to) expresses personal obligation, and savoir (to know) expresses knowledge or a learned skill — different from connaître (to be familiar with a place/person), which you'll see later on.
examples: I know how to speak French.

blocks.title: Il faut: an impersonal alternative to devoir
blocks.body: Il faut + infinitive expresses a need or a general rule — without saying WHO has to do something. Il faut never conjugates; it's always the same form. Devoir + infinitive, on the other hand, is personal: you conjugate the verb to say that ONE specific person has to do something (je dois, tu dois, il doit...). Compare the two examples: the first is a general rule, the second is aimed at a specific person.
examples: You have to sleep eight hours. (general rule, applies to anyone)
You need to rest. (directed at you specifically)

blocks.title: Très bien! 🎉
blocks.body: Four essential verbs — all irregular, so it's worth memorizing the whole table. Remember: il faut isn't in the table because it doesn't conjugate; it's always invariable.

review.why: English 'can' is a modal with no infinitive; glossed with both forms
FR 'vous' formal/plural; EN 'you' has no formal/plural distinction

review.en: You have to sleep eight hours.
review.why: impersonal 'il faut' rendered with generic 'you' (more natural in English than 'one must')
